questions.question: The workdone in an adiabatic change in an ideal gas depends upon only :
questions.explanation:
For an adiabatic process, the work done is given by the change in internal energy:

$$
\Delta W = -\Delta U
$$

For an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is directly proportional to the change in temperature:

$$
\Delta U = nC_{V}\Delta T
$$

Therefore, the work done in an adiabatic change in an ideal gas depends only on the change in its temperature:

$$
\Delta W = -nC_{V}\Delta T
$$

questions.question: A container of fixed volume contains a gas at 27$^{\circ}$C. To double the pressure of the gas, the temperature of gas should be raised to $^{\circ}$C.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For a fixed volume, the pressure of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac's Law). Therefore, we can write:

$$
\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}
$$

Given initial temperature \(T_1 = 27^{\circ}C = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}\). Let initial pressure be \(P_1 = P\). The final pressure is \(P_2 = 2P\) (double the pressure).

$$
\frac{P}{300} = \frac{2P}{T_2}
$$

Solving for \(T_2\):

$$
T_2 = 2 \times 300 \text{ K}
$$

$$
T_2 = 600 \text{ K}
$$

To convert from Kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273:

$$
T_2 = 600 - 273
$$

$$
T_2 = 327^{\circ}C
$$

questions.question: The expression given below shows the variation of velocity (v) with time (t), v = $At^2 + \frac{Bt}{C + t}$ The dimension of ABC is :
questions.explanation:
According to the principle of homogeneity of dimensions, the dimensions of each term in an equation must be the same.

Given equation: \(v = At^2 + \frac{Bt}{C + t}\)

Dimension of velocity \(v = [LT^{-1}]\)

Dimension of time \(t = [T]\)

Since C is added to t, their dimensions must be the same.

$$
[C] = [T]
$$

Dimension of \(At^2\) must be equal to the dimension of \(v\).

$$
[A][T^2] = [LT^{-1}]
$$

$$
[A] = [LT^{-1}][T^{-2}] = [LT^{-3}]
$$

Dimension of \(\frac{Bt}{C+t}\) must be equal to the dimension of \(v\).

Since \([C+t] = [T]\), we have:

$$
\frac{[B][T]}{[T]} = [LT^{-1}]
$$

$$
[B] = [LT^{-1}]
$$

Now, multiply the dimensions of A, B, and C:

$$
[ABC] = [A][B][C]
$$

$$
[ABC] = [LT^{-3}] \times [LT^{-1}] \times [T]
$$

$$
[ABC] = [L^{1+1} T^{-3-1+1}]
$$

$$
[ABC] = [L^2T^{-3}]
$$

The dimension of ABC is \([M^0L^2T^{-3}]\).

questions.question: The pair of physical quantities not having same dimensions is :
questions.explanation:
Let's analyze the dimensions of each pair:

• Torque (\(\tau\)) and Energy (\(E\)):
• \( [\tau] = [\text{Force} \times \text{distance}] = [MLT^{-2} \times L] = [ML^2T^{-2}] \)
• \( [E] = [ML^2T^{-2}] \)
• Thus, \( [\tau] = [E] \). (Same dimensions)

• Surface tension (\(\sigma\)) and Impulse (\(I\)):
• \( [\sigma] = [\text{Force} / \text{length}] = [MLT^{-2} / L] = [MT^{-2}] \)
• \( [I] = [\text{Force} \times \text{time}] = [MLT^{-2} \times T] = [MLT^{-1}] \)
• Thus, \( [\sigma] \neq [I] \). (Different dimensions)

• Angular momentum (\(L\)) and Planck's constant (\(h\)):
• \( [L] = [\text{Moment of inertia} \times \text{angular velocity}] = [MR^2 \times T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}] \)
• \( [h] = [\text{Energy} / \text{frequency}] = [ML^2T^{-2} / T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}] \)
• Thus, \( [L] = [h] \). (Same dimensions)

• Pressure (\(P\)) and Young's modulus (\(Y\)):
• \( [P] = [\text{Force} / \text{Area}] = [MLT^{-2} / L^2] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \)
• \( [Y] = [\text{Stress} / \text{Strain}] = [\text{Pressure} / \text{dimensionless}] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \)
• Thus, \( [P] = [Y] \). (Same dimensions)

The pair of physical quantities not having the same dimensions is Surface tension and Impulse.

questions.question: The coordinates of a particle with respect to origin in a given reference frame is (1, 1, 1) meters. If a force of $\vec{F} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ acts on the particle, then the magnitude of torque (with respect to origin) in z-direction is _______.
questions.explanation:
Sol.

$$
\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
\vec{\tau} = \hat{k}(1 \times 1 - 1 \times (-1)) = \hat{k}(1 - (-1)) = \hat{k}(1+1) = 2\hat{k}
$$

$$
\vec{\tau} = \hat{i}(1 - (-1)) - \hat{j}(1 - 1) + \hat{k}(-1 - 1)
$$

$$
\vec{\tau} = 2\hat{i} - 0\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}
$$

The magnitude of torque in z-direction is the coefficient of \(\hat{k}\).

$$
|\vec{\tau}_{z}| = |-2| = 2\text{Nm}
$$

questions.question: In a hydraulic lift, the surface area of the input piston is $6 \text{ cm}^2$ and that of the output piston is $1500 \text{ cm}^2$. If $100 \text{ N}$ force is applied to the input piston to raise the output piston by $20 \text{ cm}$, then the work done is _________ kJ.
questions.explanation:
According to Pascal's principle, the pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and the walls of the containing vessel. In a hydraulic lift, this means the pressure exerted on the input piston is equal to the pressure exerted by the output piston.

$$
\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}
$$

Given values are:

• Input force \(F_1 = 100 \text{ N}\)
• Input piston area \(A_1 = 6 \text{ cm}^2\)
• Output piston area \(A_2 = 1500 \text{ cm}^2\)
• Displacement of output piston \(S = 20 \text{ cm}\)

Using the principle of hydraulic lift:

$$
\frac{100}{6} = \frac{F}{1500}
$$

Solving for \(F\):

$$
F = \frac{100}{6} \times 1500 = \frac{50}{3} \times 1500
$$

$$
F = 50 \times 500 = 25 \times 10^3 \text{ N}
$$

Work done (\(\omega\)) is given by the product of force and displacement. The displacement needs to be in meters.

$$
\omega = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{S}
$$

Convert displacement from cm to m: \(20 \text{ cm} = \frac{20}{100} \text{ m} = 0.2 \text{ m}\).

$$
\omega = (25 \times 10^3 \text{ N}) \times (\frac{20}{100} \text{ m})
$$

$$
\omega = 25 \times 10^3 \times 0.2 = 5 \times 10^3 \text{ J}
$$

Convert work done from Joules to kilojoules (kJ):

$$
\omega = 5 \times 10^3 \text{ J} = 5 \text{ kJ}
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). **Assertion (A)** : Time period of a simple pendulum is longer at the top of a mountain than that at the base of the mountain. **Reason (R)** : Time period of a simple pendulum decreases with increasing value of acceleration due to gravity and vice-versa. In the light of the above statements, choose the **most appropriate** answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is **not** the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
As height (h) increases, the acceleration due to gravity (g) decreases. The time period (T) of a simple pendulum is given by the formula:

$$
T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}
$$

From the formula, it is clear that the time period \(T\) is inversely proportional to the square root of \(g\) (\(T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}\)). Therefore, as \(g\) decreases, \(T\) increases.

The variation of \(g\) with height is given by:

$$
g = \frac{g_{0}R^{2}}{(R + h)^{2}}
$$

At the top of a mountain, \(h > 0\), so \(g\) is less than at the base (\(h=0\)). A smaller \(g\) results in a longer time period \(T\). Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) states that the time period decreases with an increasing value of \(g\), which is consistent with the formula \(T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}\). So, Reason (R) is also true.

Since the decrease in \(g\) with height is the reason for the increase in the time period, Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).

questions.question: Two projectiles are fired with same initial speed from same point on ground at angles of $(45^\circ - \alpha)$ and $(45^\circ + \alpha)$, respectively, with the horizontal direction. The ratio of their maximum heights attained is :
questions.explanation:
The maximum height \(H_{\text{Max}}\) for a projectile launched with initial speed \(u\) at an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal is given by:

$$
H_{\text{Max}} = \frac{(u\sin\theta)^2}{2g}
$$

For the two projectiles, the initial speed \(u\) and acceleration due to gravity \(g\) are the same. The angles of projection are \(\theta_1 = (45^\circ - \alpha)\) and \(\theta_2 = (45^\circ + \alpha)\).

The ratio of their maximum heights is:

$$
\frac{(H_{\text{max}})_1}{(H_{\text{max}})_2} = \frac{u^2 \sin^2 (45^\circ - \alpha)}{u^2 \sin^2 (45^\circ + \alpha)}
$$

$$
= \frac{\sin^2 (45^\circ - \alpha)}{\sin^2 (45^\circ + \alpha)}
$$

Using the trigonometric identity \(\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B\):

$$
\sin(45^\circ - \alpha) = \sin 45^\circ \cos \alpha - \cos 45^\circ \sin \alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos \alpha - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin \alpha
$$

$$
\sin(45^\circ + \alpha) = \sin 45^\circ \cos \alpha + \cos 45^\circ \sin \alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos \alpha + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin \alpha
$$

Substitute these into the ratio:

$$
= \frac{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos \alpha - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin \alpha\right)^2}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos \alpha + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin \alpha\right)^2}
$$

$$
= \frac{\frac{1}{2}(\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha)^2}{\frac{1}{2}(\cos \alpha + \sin \alpha)^2}
$$

$$
= \frac{(\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha)^2}{(\cos \alpha + \sin \alpha)^2}
$$

Expand the squares:

$$
= \frac{\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha - 2\sin \alpha \cos \alpha}{\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha + 2\sin \alpha \cos \alpha}
$$

Using the identities \(\cos^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \alpha = 1\) and \(2\sin \alpha \cos \alpha = \sin 2\alpha\):

$$
= \frac{1 - \sin 2\alpha}{1 + \sin 2\alpha}
$$

questions.question: The fractional compression $$\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)  of water at the depth of 2.5 km below the sea level is ______ %. Given, the Bulk modulus of water = $2 \times 10^9 \text{ Nm}^{-2}$, density of water = $10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, acceleration due to gravity = $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$.
questions.explanation:
The Bulk modulus (B) is defined as the ratio of pressure change (\(\Delta P\)) to the fractional change in volume (\(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\)).

$$
B = \frac{\Delta P}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}
$$

The pressure at a depth h below the sea level is given by \(\Delta P = \rho gh\).

Substituting this into the Bulk modulus formula:

$$
B = \frac{\rho gh}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}
$$

We need to find the fractional compression as a percentage, so we rearrange the formula:

$$
\frac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100 = \frac{\rho gh}{B} \times 100
$$

Given values:

• Density of water (\(\rho\)) = \(10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3}\)
• Acceleration due to gravity (g) = \(10 \text{ ms}^{-2}\)
• Depth (h) = 2.5 km = \(2.5 \times 10^3 \text{ m}\)
• Bulk modulus (B) = \(2 \times 10^9 \text{ Nm}^{-2}\)

Substitute the values into the equation:

$$
\frac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100 = \frac{1000 \times 10 \times 2.5 \times 10^3}{2 \times 10^9} \times 100\%
$$

$$
= \frac{2.5 \times 10^7}{2 \times 10^9} \times 100\%
$$

$$
= 1.25 \times 10^{-2} \times 100\%
$$

$$
= 1.25\%
$$

questions.question: Consider $I_1$ and $I_2$ are the currents flowing simultaneously in two nearby coils 1 & 2, respectively. If $L_1$ = self inductance of coil 1, $M_{12}$ = mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2, then the value of induced emf in coil 1 will be
questions.explanation:
The total magnetic flux \(\phi_1\) linked with coil 1 is due to its own current \(I_1\) and the current \(I_2\) in the nearby coil 2. Thus,

$$
\phi_1 = L_1 I_1 + M_{12} I_2
$$

According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the induced emf \(\varepsilon_1\) in coil 1 is given by the negative rate of change of magnetic flux:

$$
\varepsilon_1 = -\frac{d\phi_1}{dt}
$$

Substituting the expression for \(\phi_1\) and differentiating with respect to time:

$$
\varepsilon_1 = -\frac{d}{dt}(L_1 I_1 + M_{12} I_2)
$$

$$
\varepsilon_1 = -L_1 \frac{dI_1}{dt} - M_{12} \frac{dI_2}{dt}
$$

This matches option (3).

questions.question: If $\lambda$ and K are de Broglie Wavelength and kinetic energy, respectively, of a particle with constant mass. The correct graphical representation for the particle will be :-
questions.explanation:
$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}
$$

From the de Broglie wavelength formula, we have:

$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}
$$

Squaring both sides:

$$
\lambda^2 = \frac{h^2}{2mK}
$$

Rearranging to express \(\frac{1}{K}\) in terms of \(\lambda\):

$$
\frac{1}{K} = \frac{2m}{h^2} \lambda^2
$$

Let \(Y = \frac{1}{K}\) and \(X = \lambda\). The equation becomes \(Y = cX^2\), where \(c = \frac{2m}{h^2}\) is a positive constant (since m and h are positive constants).

This equation represents an upward-facing parabola that passes through the origin (since when \(\lambda = 0\), \(\frac{1}{K} = 0\)).

Graph (2) correctly depicts an upward-facing parabolic curve starting from the origin, with \(\frac{1}{K}\) on the y-axis and \(\lambda\) on the x-axis.

Let u and v be the distances of the object and the image from a lens of focal length f. The correct graphical representation of u and v for a convex lens when $|u| > f$, is
questions.explanation:
For a convex lens, the relationship between object distance \(u\), image distance \(v\), and focal length \(f\) is given by the lens formula. Using the Cartesian sign convention where \(u\) is negative for a real object and \(v\) is positive for a real image, the lens formula is:

$$
\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}
$$

From this, we can express \(v\) in terms of \(u\) and \(f\):

$$
\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{u+f}{uf}
$$

$$
v = \frac{uf}{u+f}
$$

The problem states that \(|u| > f\). Since \(u\) is the object distance for a real object, it is negative. So, the condition \(|u| > f\) implies \(u < -f\).

Let's analyze the behavior of \(v\) for \(u < -f\):

• As \(u \to -f^-\), meaning \(u\) approaches \(-f\) from the left (i.e., \(u\) is more negative than \(-f\)), the denominator \((u+f)\) approaches \(0^-\). The numerator \(uf\) approaches \((-f)f = -f^2\). Therefore, \(v = \frac{-f^2}{0^-} \to +\infty\).
• As \(u \to -\infty\), we can rewrite \(v = \frac{f}{1 + f/u}\). As \(u \to -\infty\), \(f/u \to 0\). Therefore, \(v \to \frac{f}{1+0} = f\).

Thus, the graph of \(v\) versus \(u\) for a convex lens when \(u < -f\) should show \(v\) starting from \(+\infty\) as \(u\) approaches \(-f\) from the left, and decreasing asymptotically towards \(v = f\) as \(u\) tends to \(-\infty\). This behavior is characteristic of a rectangular hyperbola with asymptotes at \(u = -f\) and \(v = f\).

Comparing this with the given options, Graph (2) correctly depicts this behavior.

The solution also provides Newton's formula for lenses, which is a common alternative form of the lens equation:

$$
(u + f)(v - f) = f^2
$$

This equation also describes a hyperbola with asymptotes at \(u = -f\) and \(v = f\) when \(u\) and \(v\) are distances from the optical center. The provided solution diagram illustrates a similar hyperbolic curve, typically plotting \(v\) against the magnitude of the object distance \(|u|\) on the positive x-axis, with asymptotes at \(|u| = f\) and \(v = f\).

questions.question: An electric dipole of mass m, charge q, and length $l$ is placed in a uniform electric field $\vec{E} = E_0 \hat{i}$. When the dipole is rotated slightly from its equilibrium position and released, the time period of its oscillations will be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For a dipole in a uniform electric field, the restoring torque \(\tau = -pE\sin\theta\). For small oscillations, \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\).

The dipole moment is \(p = ql\). So, \(\tau = -qlE_0\theta\).

The equation of motion for angular SHM is \(I\ddot{\theta} = \tau\).

$$
I\ddot{\theta} = -qlE_0\theta
$$

Comparing this with \(I\ddot{\theta} = -k\theta\), we get the angular spring constant \(k = qlE_0\).

The moment of inertia \(I\) of the dipole (two point masses \(m\) at \(l/2\) from the center) about its center is:

$$
I = m\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 + m\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 = 2m\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 = 2m\frac{l^2}{4} = \frac{ml^2}{2}
$$

The angular frequency of oscillation is given by \(\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{I}}\).

$$
\omega^2 = \frac{k}{I} = \frac{qlE_0}{ml^2/2} = \frac{2qlE_0}{ml^2} = \frac{2qE_0}{ml}
$$

The time period \(T\) is related to the angular frequency by \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\).

$$
T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{ml}{2qE_0}}
$$

questions.question: A coil of area A and N turns is rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ about an axis perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. Magnetic flux $\phi$ and induced emf $\varepsilon$ across it, at an instant when $\vec{B}$ is parallel to the plane of coil, are :
questions.explanation:
The magnetic flux \(\phi\) through a coil of N turns and area A, rotating with angular velocity \(\omega\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), is given by:

$$
\phi = NBA \cos(\theta)
$$

Where \(\theta\) is the angle between the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) and the normal to the plane of the coil. If the coil starts rotating from a position where its normal is parallel to \(\vec{B}\), then \(\theta = \omega t\).

$$
\phi = NBA \cos(\omega t)
$$

The induced electromotive force (emf) \(\varepsilon\) is given by Faraday's law of induction:

$$
\varepsilon = -\frac{d\phi}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the flux expression with respect to time:

$$
\varepsilon = -\frac{d}{dt}(NBA \cos(\omega t)) = -NBA(-\sin(\omega t))\omega = NBA\omega \sin(\omega t)
$$

We are asked to find \(\phi\) and \(\varepsilon\) at an instant when \(\vec{B}\) is parallel to the plane of the coil. When \(\vec{B}\) is parallel to the plane of the coil, the angle between \(\vec{B}\) and the normal to the plane of the coil is \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (or \(90^{\circ}\)). Therefore, \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Substitute \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) into the expressions for \(\phi\) and \(\varepsilon\):

$$
\phi = NBA \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = NBA(0) = 0
$$

$$
\varepsilon = NBA\omega \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = NBA\omega (1) = NBA\omega
$$

Thus, when \(\vec{B}\) is parallel to the plane of the coil, the magnetic flux is \(\phi = 0\) and the induced emf is \(\varepsilon = NBA\omega\).

questions.question: As shown below, bob A of a pendulum having massless string of length 'R' is released from $60^{\circ}$ to the vertical. It hits another bob B of half the mass that is at rest on a friction less table in the centre. Assuming elastic collision, the magnitude of the velocity of bob A after the collision will be (take g as acceleration due to gravity)
questions.explanation:
Velocity of A just before hitting:

$$
u = \sqrt{2g\frac{R}{2}} = \sqrt{gR}
$$

Just after collision, let velocity of A and B be \(v_{1}\) and \(v_{2}\) respectively.

By Conservation of Momentum (COM):

$$
mu = mv_{1} + \frac{m}{2}v_{2}
$$

Dividing by m and multiplying by 2:

$$
2u = 2v_{1} + v_{2} \quad \ldots(i)
$$

For elastic collision, the coefficient of restitution \(e = 1\):

$$
e = 1 = \frac{v_{2} - v_{1}}{u}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow v_{2} - v_{1} = u \quad \ldots(ii)
$$

Subtract equation (ii) from equation (i):

$$
(2v_{1} + v_{2}) - (v_{2} - v_{1}) = 2u - u
$$

$$
3v_{1} = u
$$

$$
\Rightarrow v_{1} = \frac{u}{3}
$$

Substitute the value of \(u\) from Step 1:

$$
v_{1} = \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{gR}
$$

questions.question: At the interface between two materials having refractive indices $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$, the critical angle for reflection of an em wave is $\theta_{1C}$. The $n_{2}$ material is replaced by another material having refractive index $n_{3}$, such that the critical angle at the interface between $n_{1}$ and $n_{3}$ materials is $\theta_{2C}$. If $n_{3} > n_{2} > n_{1}$; $\frac${$n_{2}$}{$n_{3}$} = $\frac{2}{5} \text{ and } \sin \$theta_{2C}  - $\sin \$theta_{1C}  = $\frac{1}{2} \text{, then } \$theta_{1C}  $\text{ is}$
questions.explanation:
The critical angle \(\theta_{C}\) for total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser medium (higher refractive index) to a rarer medium (lower refractive index). The formula is \(\sin\theta_{C} = \frac{n_{rarer}}{n_{denser}}\).

Given \(n_{3} > n_{2} > n_{1}\), \(n_{1}\) is the rarer medium in both scenarios.

For the interface between materials with indices \(n_{1}\) and \(n_{2}\), the critical angle \(\theta_{1C}\) is given by:

$$
\sin\theta_{1C} = \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}
$$

For the interface between materials with indices \(n_{1}\) and \(n_{3}\), the critical angle \(\theta_{2C}\) is given by:

$$
\sin\theta_{2C} = \frac{n_{1}}{n_{3}}
$$

We are given the relation:

$$
\sin\theta_{2C} - \sin\theta_{1C} = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Substituting the expressions for the sines of the critical angles:

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{3}} - \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Factoring out \(n_{1}\):

$$
n_{1}\left(\frac{1}{n_{3}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
n_{1}\left(\frac{n_{2} - n_{3}}{n_{2}n_{3}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

To use the given ratio \(\frac{n_{2}}{n_{3}} = \frac{2}{5}\), we can rewrite the equation as:

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}\left(\frac{n_{2} - n_{3}}{n_{3}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}\left(\frac{n_{2}}{n_{3}} - 1\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Now, substitute \(\frac{n_{2}}{n_{3}} = \frac{2}{5}\):

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}\left(\frac{2}{5} - 1\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = -\frac{5}{6}
$$

Since \(\sin\theta_{1C} = \frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}\), we have:

$$
\sin\theta_{1C} = -\frac{5}{6}
$$

questions.question: Two light beams fall on a transparent material block at point 1 and 2 with angle $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, respectively, as shown in figure. After refraction, the beams intersect at point 3 which is exactly on the interface at other end of the block. Given : the distance between 1 and 2, $d=4\sqrt{3}$ cm and $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = \cos^{-1} \left$($\frac{$n_2$}{$2n_1$} \right$) , where refractive index of the block $n_2 \gt$ refractive index of the outside medium $n_1$, then the thickness of the block is ______ cm.
questions.explanation:
From Snell's law at point 1 (or 2), considering the angle with the normal:

$$
n_1 \sin(90 - \theta_1) = n_2 \sin \theta_3
$$

$$
n_1 \cos \theta_1 = n_2 \sin \theta_3
$$

Given \(\theta_1 = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{n_2}{2n_1}\right)\), which implies \(\cos \theta_1 = \frac{n_2}{2n_1}\). Substitute this into the Snell's law equation:

$$
n_1 \left(\frac{n_2}{2n_1}\right) = n_2 \sin \theta_3
$$

$$
\frac{n_2}{2} = n_2 \sin \theta_3
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2} = \sin \theta_3
$$

Therefore, the angle of refraction \(\theta_3\) is:

$$
\theta_3 = 30^{\circ}
$$

From the diagram, the horizontal distance covered by each refracted ray inside the block until it reaches the midpoint of the base (point 3) is \(d/2\). Let 't' be the thickness of the block. In the right-angled triangle formed by the refracted ray, the normal, and the horizontal line to point 3:

$$
\tan \theta_3 = \frac{\text{horizontal distance}}{\text{vertical distance}} = \frac{d/2}{t}
$$

$$
\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{d}{2t}
$$

We know \(\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). So,

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{d}{2t}
$$

Rearranging for 't':

$$
t = \frac{d\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

Given \(d = 4\sqrt{3}\) cm. Substitute this value into the equation for 't':

$$
t = \frac{(4\sqrt{3})\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ cm}
$$

$$
t = \frac{4 \times 3}{2} \text{ cm}
$$

$$
t = \frac{12}{2} \text{ cm}
$$

$$
t = 6 \text{ cm}
$$

questions.question: Choose the correct statements. (A) Weight of a substance is the amount of matter present in it. (B) Mass is the force exerted by gravity on an object. (C) Volume is the amount of space occupied by a substance. (D) Temperatures below $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ are possible in Celsius scale, but in Kelvin scale negative temperature is not possible. (E) Precision refers to the closeness of various measurements for the same quantity.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Let's analyze each statement:

• **(A) Weight of a substance is the amount of matter present in it.** This statement is incorrect. Weight is the force exerted by gravity on an object, while the amount of matter present in it is called mass.
• **(B) Mass is the force exerted by gravity on an object.** This statement is incorrect. Mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object, whereas the force exerted by gravity on an object is its weight.
• **(C) Volume is the amount of space occupied by a substance.** This statement is correct. This is the standard definition of volume.
• **(D) Temperatures below \(0^{\circ}\text{C}\) are possible in Celsius scale, but in Kelvin scale negative temperature is not possible.** This statement is correct. The Celsius scale allows for negative temperatures (e.g., \(-10^{\circ}\text{C}\)), but the Kelvin scale is an absolute temperature scale where the lowest possible temperature is 0 K (absolute zero), meaning negative Kelvin temperatures are not possible.
• **(E) Precision refers to the closeness of various measurements for the same quantity.** This statement is correct. Precision describes how close multiple measurements of the same item are to each other.

Therefore, the correct statements are (C), (D), and (E).

questions.question: The molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte when plotted against the square root of its concentration, which of the following is expected to be observed?
options: A small decrease in molar conductivity is observed at infinite dilution.
A small increase in molar conductivity is observed at infinite dilution.
Molar conductivity increases sharply with increase in concentration.
Molar conductivity decreases sharply with increase in concentration.
questions.explanation:
For a weak electrolyte, the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) is low at high concentrations and increases significantly upon dilution. Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) is directly proportional to the number of ions in the solution. As concentration increases, the degree of dissociation decreases, leading to a decrease in the number of ions per unit volume, and thus a decrease in molar conductivity.

When molar conductivity is plotted against the square root of concentration (\(\sqrt{C}\)) for a weak electrolyte, the graph shows a sharp decrease in molar conductivity as concentration increases (i.e., as \(\sqrt{C}\) increases). This is because the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte decreases with increasing concentration.

questions.question: If $a_{0}$ is denoted as the Bohr radius of hydrogen atom, then what is the de-Broglie wavelength  \left(\lambda\right)$$ of the electron present in the second orbit of hydrogen atom ? [n : any integer]
questions.explanation:
According to Bohr's quantization condition for angular momentum, for an electron in the \(n^{th}\) orbit, the circumference of the orbit is an integral multiple of the de-Broglie wavelength:

$$
2\pi r_{n} = n\lambda
$$

For a hydrogen atom, the radius of the \(n^{th}\) orbit is given by \(r_{n} = n^{2}a_{0}\). For the second orbit, \(n=2\), so:

$$
r_{2} = (2)^{2}a_{0} = 4a_{0}
$$

Substitute \(r_{2} = 4a_{0}\) into the de-Broglie wavelength equation:

$$
2\pi (4a_{0}) = n\lambda
$$

$$
8\pi a_{0} = n\lambda
$$

Solving for \(\lambda\):

$$
\lambda = \frac{8\pi a_{0}}{n}
$$

questions.question: 500 J of energy is transferred as heat to 0.5 mol of Argon gas at 298 K and 1.00 atm. The final temperature and the change in internal energy respectively are : Given : $R = 8.3 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$
questions.explanation:
For a constant pressure process, heat transferred \(q_{p} = \Delta H\).

For a monatomic ideal gas (Argon), the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is \(C_{p} = \frac{5}{2}R\) and at constant volume is \(C_{v} = \frac{3}{2}R\).

$$
q_{p} = n \times C_{p} \times \Delta T
$$

$$
500 = 0.5 \times \frac{5}{2} \times 8.3 \times (T_{f}-298)
$$

$$
500 = 0.5 \times 2.5 \times 8.3 \times (T_{f}-298)
$$

$$
500 = 10.375 \times (T_{f}-298)
$$

$$
T_{f}-298 = \frac{500}{10.375} \approx 48.19
$$

$$
T_{f} \approx 298 + 48.19 = 346.19 \text{ K}
$$

Rounding off, \(T_{f} \approx 346 \text{ K}\) or \(348 \text{ K}\) as per options.

Now, calculate the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\).

We know that \(\Delta U = n C_{v} \Delta T\).

Alternatively, we can use the relationship between \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\) for an ideal gas:

$$
\Delta H = \Delta U + nR \Delta T
$$

Or, using the ratio of heat capacities:

$$
\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta U} = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}} = \frac{\frac{5}{2}R}{\frac{3}{2}R} = \frac{5}{3}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{3}{5} \times \Delta H
$$

Since \(\Delta H = q_{p} = 500 \text{ J}\) (heat transferred at constant pressure):

$$
\Delta U = \frac{3}{5} \times 500 = 300 \text{ J}
$$

Thus, the final temperature is approximately \(346.2 \text{ K}\) (closest to \(348 \text{ K}\)) and the change in internal energy is \(300 \text{ J}\).

questions.question: At temperature $T$, compound $AB_{2(g)}$ dissociates as $AB_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons AB_{(g)} + \frac{1}{2}B_{2(g)}$ having degree of dissociation $x$ (small compared to unity). The correct expression for $x$ in terms of $K_{p}$ and $p$ is
questions.explanation:
The given dissociation reaction is:

$$
AB_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons AB_{(g)} + \frac{1}{2}B_{2(g)}
$$

Initial moles:

$$
\begin{array}{lccc} & AB_{2(g)} & AB_{(g)} & B_{2(g)} \\ \text{Initial} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{At eq.} & 1-x & x & x/2 \end{array}
$$

Total moles at equilibrium \(n_{\text{total}} = (1-x) + x + \frac{x}{2} = 1 + \frac{x}{2}\).

Let the total pressure be \(P\). The partial pressures are:

$$
P_{AB_2} = \frac{1-x}{1+x/2} P
$$

$$
P_{AB} = \frac{x}{1+x/2} P
$$

$$
P_{B_2} = \frac{x/2}{1+x/2} P
$$

Given that \(x\) is small compared to unity (\(x \ll 1\)), we can approximate:

$$
1 + \frac{x}{2} \approx 1 \quad \text{and} \quad 1 - x \approx 1
$$

So, the partial pressures become:

$$
P_{AB_2} \approx P
$$

$$
P_{AB} \approx xP
$$

$$
P_{B_2} \approx \frac{x}{2}P
$$

The equilibrium constant \(K_p\) is given by:

$$
K_{p} = \frac{P_{AB} \cdot P_{B_2}^{1/2}}{P_{AB_2}}
$$

Substitute the approximate partial pressures into the \(K_p\) expression:

$$
K_{p} = \frac{(xP) \cdot \left(\frac{xP}{2}\right)^{1/2}}{P}
$$

Simplify the expression:

$$
K_{p} = xP \cdot \frac{x^{1/2} P^{1/2}}{\sqrt{2} P}
$$

$$
K_{p} = \frac{x^{3/2} P^{1/2}}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

Square both sides:

$$
K_{p}^{2} = \frac{x^3 P}{2}
$$

Rearrange to solve for \(x^3\):

$$
x^3 = \frac{2K_{p}^{2}}{P}
$$

Take the cube root to find \(x\):

$$
x = \sqrt[3]{\frac{2K_{p}^{2}}{P}}
$$

questions.question: The reaction $A_{2} + B_{2} \to 2 AB$ follows the mechanism $A_{2} \underset${$k_{-1}$}{$\overset${$k_{1}$}{$\rightleftharpoons$}} A + A(fast) A + $B_{2} \xrightarrow${$k_{2}$} AB + B (slow) A + B \to AB (fast) The overall order of the reaction is :
questions.explanation:
From the slow step, the rate law is:

$$
\text{rate} = k_{2}[A][B_{2}] \quad ......(1)
$$

From the fast equilibrium step:

$$
A_{2} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_{1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} A + A
$$

At equilibrium, the rate of forward reaction equals the rate of reverse reaction:

$$
k_{1}[A_{2}] = k_{-1}[A]^{2}
$$

$$
\left(\frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}\right) = \left(\frac{[A]^{2}}{[A_{2}]}\right)
$$

Solving for \([A]\):

$$
[A]^{2} = \frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}[A_{2}]
$$

$$
\Rightarrow [A] = \sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}} \cdot \sqrt{[A_{2}]}
$$

Substituting this expression for \([A]\) into equation (1):

$$
\text{Rate} = k_{2}\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}} \cdot [A_{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot [B_{2}]
$$

Combining the constants, let \(k' = k_{2}\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}}\):

$$
\text{Rate} = k'[A_{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}} [B_{2}]^{1}
$$

The overall order of the reaction is the sum of the exponents of the concentration terms in the rate law:

$$
\therefore \text{order} = \frac{1}{2} + 1 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 1.5
$$

questions.question: The number of solutions of the equation $\left(\frac{9}{x} - \frac{9}{\sqrt{x}} + 2\right) \left(\frac{2}{x} - \frac{7}{\sqrt{x}} + 3\right)$ = 0 is :
questions.explanation:
Consider \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = \alpha\). For this to be defined, we must have \(x > 0\).

Substituting \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = \alpha\) into the equation, we get \(\frac{1}{x} = \alpha^2\).

$$
\{9\alpha^2 - 9\alpha + 2\}\{2\alpha^2 - 7\alpha + 3\} = 0
$$

Factorizing both quadratic expressions:

$$
(3\alpha - 2)(3\alpha - 1)(\alpha - 3)(2\alpha - 1) = 0
$$

Setting each factor to zero, we find the possible values for \(\alpha\):

$$
\alpha = \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, 3, \frac{1}{2}
$$

Now, we use \(x = \frac{1}{\alpha^2}\) to find the corresponding values of \(x\):

$$
x = \frac{1}{(2/3)^2} = \frac{9}{4}
$$

$$
x = \frac{1}{(1/3)^2} = 9
$$

$$
x = \frac{1}{(3)^2} = \frac{1}{9}
$$

$$
x = \frac{1}{(1/2)^2} = 4
$$

So, the values of \(x\) are \(9, 4, \frac{9}{4}, \frac{1}{9}\).

All these values are positive, satisfying the condition \(x > 0\).

Therefore, there are 4 distinct solutions.

questions.question: Define a relation R on the interval $[0, \frac{\pi}{2})$ by x R y if and only if $\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y = 1$. Then R is :
options: both reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
both reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric not transitive
questions.explanation:
The given relation is \(x R y\) if and only if \(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y = 1\) on the interval \([0, \frac{\pi}{2})\).

For the relation to be reflexive, \(x R x\) must hold for all \(x\). We check if \(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}x = 1\).

This is a fundamental trigonometric identity, so it is always true. Thus, the relation R is reflexive.

Assume \(x R y\) is true, which means \(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y = 1\). We need to check if \(y R x\) is true, i.e., if \(\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}x = 1\).

From \(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y = 1\), using \(\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x\), we get:

$$
(1 + \tan^{2}x) - \tan^{2}y = 1 \Rightarrow \tan^{2}x = \tan^{2}y
$$

Now, let's evaluate \(\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}x\):

$$
\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}x = (1 + \tan^{2}y) - \tan^{2}x
$$

Since \(\tan^{2}y = \tan^{2}x\), we have:

$$
(1 + \tan^{2}x) - \tan^{2}x = 1
$$

Thus, \(y R x\) is true. The relation R is symmetric.

Assume \(x R y\) and \(y R z\) are true. This gives us two equations:

$$
\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y = 1 \quad (i)
$$

$$
\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}z = 1 \quad (ii)
$$

Adding equations (i) and (ii):

$$
(\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}y) + (\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}z) = 1 + 1
$$

$$
\sec^{2}x + (\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}y) - \tan^{2}z = 2
$$

Using the identity \(\sec^{2}y - \tan^{2}y = 1\):

$$
\sec^{2}x + 1 - \tan^{2}z = 2
$$

$$
\sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}z = 1
$$

This shows that \(x R z\) is true. Thus, the relation R is transitive.

Since the relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, it is an equivalence relation.

questions.question: The least value of n for which the number of integral terms in the Binomial expansion of $\left(\sqrt[3]{7} + \sqrt[12]{11}\right)$^n is 183, is :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The general term \(T_{r+1}\) in the binomial expansion of \((\sqrt[3]{7} + \sqrt[12]{11})^n\) is given by:

$$
T_{r+1} = {}^{n}C_{r} \left(7^{1/3}\right)^{n-r} \left(11^{1/12}\right)^{r}
$$

$$
T_{r+1} = {}^{n}C_{r} 7^{\frac{n-r}{3}} 11^{\frac{r}{12}}
$$

For \(T_{r+1}\) to be an integral term, the powers of 7 and 11 must be non-negative integers. This means \(\frac{n-r}{3}\) and \(\frac{r}{12}\) must both be integers.

From the condition that \(\frac{r}{12}\) must be an integer, \(r\) must be a multiple of 12. Let \(r = 12k\), where \(k\) is a non-negative integer (\(k \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}\)).

Also, we know that \(0 \le r \le n\).

The problem states that there are 183 integral terms. Since \(r = 12k\), the possible values of \(r\) are \(0, 12, 24, \dots, 12k_{max}\).

The number of such terms is \(k_{max} + 1\). Given that the number of integral terms is 183:

$$
k_{max} + 1 = 183
$$

$$
k_{max} = 182
$$

Now, we can find the maximum value of \(r\):

$$
r_{max} = 12 \times k_{max} = 12 \times 182
$$

$$
r_{max} = 2184
$$

Since \(0 \le r \le n\), the maximum value of \(r\) must be less than or equal to \(n\). Therefore, \(n \ge r_{max}\).

The least value of \(n\) for which \(r_{max} = 2184\) is possible is when \(n = r_{max}\).

Thus, the least value of \(n = 2184\).

questions.question: Let $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. Let $L_1$ : $\vec{r}$ = (-$\hat{i}$ + 2$\hat{j} + \hat{k}$) + $\lambda \vec{a}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R} L_2$ : $\vec{r}$ = ($\hat{j} + \hat{k}$) + $\mu \vec{b}$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ be two lines. If the line $L_3$ passes through the point of intersection of $L_1$ and $L_2$, and is parallel to $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$, then $L_3$ passes through the point:
questions.explanation:
Given lines are:

$$
L_1 : \vec{r} = (-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \lambda \vec{a}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow L_1 : \vec{r} = (-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \vec{r} = (\lambda - 1)\hat{i} + (2 + 2\lambda)\hat{j} + (1 + \lambda)\hat{k}
$$

$$
L_2 : \vec{r} = (\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \mu \vec{b}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow L_2 : \vec{r} = (\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + \mu(2\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \vec{r} = 2\mu\hat{i} + (1 + 7\mu)\hat{j} + (1 + 3\mu)\hat{k}
$$

For the point of intersection, equating respective components:

$$
\lambda - 1 = 2\mu \quad ...(1)
$$

$$
2 + 2\lambda = 1 + 7\mu \quad ...(2)
$$

$$
1 + \lambda = 1 + 3\mu \quad ...(3)
$$

From (3), \(\lambda = 3\mu\). Substitute into (1):

$$
3\mu - 1 = 2\mu \Rightarrow \mu = 1
$$

Substitute \(\mu = 1\) into \(\lambda = 3\mu\):

$$
\lambda = 3(1) = 3
$$

Check with (2): \(2 + 2(3) = 8\) and \(1 + 7(1) = 8\). The values are consistent.

So, \(\lambda = 3\) and \(\mu = 1\).

The point of intersection (P) can be found by substituting \(\lambda = 3\) into \(L_1\) or \(\mu = 1\) into \(L_2\).

Using \(L_1\) with \(\lambda = 3\):

$$
\vec{r}_P = (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (2 + 2(3))\hat{j} + (1 + 3)\hat{k}
$$

$$
\vec{r}_P = 2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}
$$

The line \(L_3\) is parallel to \(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\).

$$
\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}) + (2\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \vec{a} + \vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}
$$

The equation of line \(L_3\) passing through \((2, 8, 4)\) and parallel to \((3\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})\) is:

$$
L_3 : \vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} + \alpha(3\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})
$$

We need to find a point that \(L_3\) passes through. Let's check the options by substituting values for \(\alpha\).

For \(\alpha = 2\):

$$
\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} + 2(3\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})
$$

$$
\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} + 6\hat{i} + 18\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}
$$

$$
\vec{r} = (2+6)\hat{i} + (8+18)\hat{j} + (4+8)\hat{k}
$$

$$
\vec{r} = 8\hat{i} + 26\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}
$$

This corresponds to the point \((8, 26, 12)\), which is option A.

questions.question: The value $of \lim_{n\to\infty} \left( \sum_{K=1}^{n} \frac{k^3 + 6k^2 + 11k + 5}{(k+3)!} \right)$ is :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k^3 + 6k^2 + 11k + 5}{(k+3)!}
$$

$$
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k^3 + 6k^2 + 11k + 6 - 1}{(k+3)!}
$$

$$
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3) - 1}{(k+3)!}
$$

$$
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left( \frac{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)}{(k+3)!} - \frac{1}{(k+3)!} \right)
$$

$$
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left( \frac{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)}{(k+3)(k+2)(k+1)k!} - \frac{1}{(k+3)!} \right)
$$

$$
= \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left( \frac{1}{k!} - \frac{1}{(k+3)!} \right)
$$

This is a telescoping sum. Let's write out the first few terms:

$$
\left( \frac{1}{1!} - \frac{1}{4!} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{2!} - \frac{1}{5!} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{3!} - \frac{1}{6!} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{4!} - \frac{1}{7!} \right) + \dots + \left( \frac{1}{n!} - \frac{1}{(n+3)!} \right)
$$

When \(n \to \infty\), the terms \(\frac{1}{(n+1)!}\), \(\frac{1}{(n+2)!}\), \(\frac{1}{(n+3)!}\) will approach 0. The sum simplifies to the first few positive terms:

$$
= \frac{1}{1!} + \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{1}{3!}
$$

$$
= 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6}
$$

$$
= \frac{6}{6} + \frac{3}{6} + \frac{1}{6}
$$

$$
= \frac{6+3+1}{6} = \frac{10}{6} = \frac{5}{3}
$$

questions.question: Let P be the set of seven digit numbers with sum of their digits equal to 11. If the numbers in P are formed by using the digits 1,2 and 3 only, then the number of elements in the set P is :
questions.explanation:
Let the seven digits be formed using only 1, 2, and 3. Let \(n_1\), \(n_2\), and \(n_3\) be the number of times digits 1, 2, and 3 appear, respectively. We have two conditions:

• Total number of digits: \(n_1 + n_2 + n_3 = 7\)
• Sum of digits: \(1 \cdot n_1 + 2 \cdot n_2 + 3 \cdot n_3 = 11\)

From the first equation, \(n_1 = 7 - n_2 - n_3\). Substitute this into the second equation:

$$
(7 - n_2 - n_3) + 2n_2 + 3n_3 = 11
$$

$$
7 + n_2 + 2n_3 = 11
$$

$$
n_2 + 2n_3 = 4
$$

Now, we find non-negative integer solutions for \(n_2\) and \(n_3\):

(i) If \(n_3 = 0\):

$$
n_2 = 4
$$

$$
n_1 = 7 - 4 - 0 = 3
$$

The digits are (1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2). Number of permutations:

$$
\frac{7!}{3!4!} = \frac{7 \times 6 \times 5}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 35
$$

(ii) If \(n_3 = 1\):

$$
n_2 + 2(1) = 4 \implies n_2 = 2
$$

$$
n_1 = 7 - 2 - 1 = 4
$$

The digits are (1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3). Number of permutations:

$$
\frac{7!}{4!2!1!} = \frac{7 \times 6 \times 5}{2 \times 1} = 105
$$

(iii) If \(n_3 = 2\):

$$
n_2 + 2(2) = 4 \implies n_2 = 0
$$

$$
n_1 = 7 - 0 - 2 = 5
$$

The digits are (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 3). Number of permutations:

$$
\frac{7!}{5!2!} = \frac{7 \times 6}{2 \times 1} = 21
$$

If \(n_3 = 3\), then \(n_2 = -2\), which is not possible.

The total number of elements in set P is the sum of permutations from all valid cases:

$$
\text{Total} = 35 + 105 + 21 = 161
$$

questions.question: The integral $80 \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \left(\frac{\sin \theta + \cos \theta}{9 + 16 \sin 2\theta}\right)$ d$\theta \text{ is equal to :}$
questions.explanation:
Let the integral be I.

$$
I = 80 \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \left(\frac{\sin \theta + \cos \theta}{9 + 16(2 \sin \theta \cos \theta)}\right) d\theta
$$

$$
= 80 \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sin \theta + \cos \theta}{9 - 16(1 - 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta - 1)} d\theta
$$

$$
= 80 \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sin \theta + \cos \theta}{9 + 16 - 16(\sin \theta - \cos \theta)^2} d\theta
$$

Let \(\sin \theta - \cos \theta = t\)

Then \((\cos \theta + \sin \theta)d\theta = dt\)

When \(\theta = 0\), \(t = \sin 0 - \cos 0 = 0 - 1 = -1\)

When \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\), \(t = \sin \frac{\pi}{4} - \cos \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\)

$$
I = 80 \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{dt}{25 - 16t^2}
$$

$$
= \frac{80}{16} \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{dt}{\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^2 - t^2}
$$

Using the formula \(\int \frac{dx}{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{2a} \ln \left| \frac{a+x}{a-x} \right|\), where \(a = \frac{5}{4}\)

$$
I = 5 \left[ \frac{1}{2 \left(\frac{5}{4}\right)} \ln \left| \frac{\frac{5}{4}+t}{\frac{5}{4}-t} \right| \right]_{-1}^{0}
$$

$$
I = 5 \left[ \frac{2}{5} \ln \left| \frac{5+4t}{5-4t} \right| \right]_{-1}^{0}
$$

$$
I = 2 \left[ \ln \left| \frac{5+4t}{5-4t} \right| \right]_{-1}^{0}
$$

$$
I = 2 \left( \ln \left| \frac{5+0}{5-0} \right| - \ln \left| \frac{5-4}{5-(-4)} \right| \right)
$$

$$
I = 2 \left( \ln(1) - \ln \left| \frac{1}{9} \right| \right)
$$

$$
I = 2 (0 - \ln(9^{-1}))
$$

$$
I = 2 (0 - (-\ln 9))
$$

$$
I = 2 \ln 9
$$

$$
I = 2 \ln (3^2)
$$

$$
I = 2 \cdot 2 \ln 3
$$

$$
I = 4 \ln 3
$$

questions.question:
Let $L_{1} : \frac{x-1}{1} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z-1}{2}$ and
$L_{2} : \frac{x+1}{-1} = \frac{y-2}{2} = \frac{z}{1}$ be two lines.
Let $L_{3}$ be a line passing through the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and be perpendicular to both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$. If $L_{3}$ intersects $L_{1}$, then $|5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma|$ equals :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The direction ratios of \(L_{1}\) are \(\vec{m} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\).

The direction ratios of \(L_{2}\) are \(\vec{n} = -\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\).

Since \(L_{3}\) is perpendicular to both \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\), its DR's are proportional to the cross product of \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{n}\).

$$
\text{DR's of } L_{3} = \vec{m} \times \vec{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
= \hat{i}(-1 - 4) - \hat{j}(1 - (-2)) + \hat{k}(2 - (-1))
$$

$$
= -5\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 1\hat{k}
$$

So, the DR's of \(L_{3}\) are \((-5, -3, 1)\).

\(L_{3}\) passes through \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) and has DR's \((-5, -3, 1)\). Its equation is:

$$
L_{3} : \frac{x-\alpha}{-5} = \frac{y-\beta}{-3} = \frac{z-\gamma}{1} = \lambda
$$

A general point on \(L_{3}\) can be represented as \(A(\alpha - 5\lambda, \beta - 3\lambda, \gamma + \lambda)\).

The equation of \(L_{1}\) is:

$$
L_{1} : \frac{x-1}{1} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z-1}{2} = k
$$

A general point on \(L_{1}\) can be represented as \(B(k+1, -k+2, 2k+1)\).

Since \(L_{3}\) intersects \(L_{1}\), the general points A and B must be the same for some values of \(\lambda\) and \(k\).

$$
\alpha - 5\lambda = k+1 \implies \alpha = 5\lambda + k + 1
$$

$$
\beta - 3\lambda = -k+2 \implies \beta = 3\lambda - k + 2
$$

$$
\gamma + \lambda = 2k+1 \implies \gamma = -\lambda + 2k + 1
$$

Substitute the expressions for \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) into \(|5\alpha - 11\beta - 8\gamma|\):

$$
5\alpha - 11\beta - 8\gamma = 5(5\lambda + k + 1) - 11(3\lambda - k + 2) - 8(-\lambda + 2k + 1)
$$

$$
= (25\lambda + 5k + 5) - (33\lambda - 11k + 22) - (-8\lambda + 16k + 8)
$$

$$
= 25\lambda + 5k + 5 - 33\lambda + 11k - 22 + 8\lambda - 16k - 8
$$

$$
= (25 - 33 + 8)\lambda + (5 + 11 - 16)k + (5 - 22 - 8)
$$

$$
= 0\lambda + 0k - 25
$$

$$
= -25
$$

Therefore, \(|5\alpha - 11\beta - 8\gamma| = |-25| = 25\).

questions.question: Let $S=\{m \in Z: A^{m^2} + A^m = 3I - A^{-6}\}$, where A = $\begin{bmatrix}$ 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 $\end{bmatrix}$ Then $n(S)$ is equal to $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$ .
questions.explanation:
Given matrix \(A\) is:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Calculate powers of \(A\):

$$
A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, A^3 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, A^4 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -4 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

and so on

$$
A^6 = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -6 \\ 6 & -5 \end{bmatrix}
$$

From the pattern, the general form for \(A^m\) is:

$$
A^m = \begin{bmatrix} m+1 & -m \\ m & -m-1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, \(A^{m^2}\) will be:

$$
A^{m^2} = \begin{bmatrix} m^2+1 & -m^2 \\ m^2 & -(m^2-1) \end{bmatrix}
$$

The given equation is \(A^{m^2} + A^m = 3I - A^{-6}\).

Substitute the expressions for \(A^{m^2}\) and \(A^m\) into the left side:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} m^2+1 & -m^2 \\ m^2 & -(m^2-1) \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} m+1 & -m \\ m & -(m-1) \end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, calculate the right side of the equation. Using the general form for \(A^m\), we find \(A^{-6}\):

$$
A^{-6} = \begin{bmatrix} -6+1 & -(-6) \\ -6 & -(-6)-1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 6 \\ -6 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the right side \(3I - A^{-6}\) is:

$$
3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 6 \\ -6 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 6 \\ -6 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -6 \\ 6 & -2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Equating the top-left elements of the matrices from both sides of the equation:

$$
(m^2+1) + (m+1) = 8
$$

$$
m^2 + m + 2 = 8
$$

$$
m^2 + m - 6 = 0
$$

Factor the quadratic equation:

$$
(m+3)(m-2) = 0
$$

This gives two possible values for \(m\):

$$
m = -3, 2
$$

Since \(m \in Z\) (integers), both values are valid. The set \(S\) is \(\{-3, 2\}\).

The number of elements in set \(S\), \(n(S)\), is 2.

questions.question: Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{10}$ be ten observations such that $\sum_{i=1}^{10} (x_i - 2) = 30$, $\sum_{i=1}^{10} (x_i - \beta)^2 = 98$, $\beta > 2$ and their variance is $\frac{4}{5}$. If $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are respectively the mean and the variance of $2(x_1-1) + 4\beta, 2(x_2-1) + 4\beta, \dots, 2(x_{10}-1) + 4\beta$, then $\frac{\beta\mu}{\sigma^2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given variance is \(\frac{4}{5}\).

$$
\frac{4}{5} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{10} - \left(\frac{\sum x_i}{10}\right)^2
$$

From \(\sum_{i=1}^{10} (x_i - 2) = 30\):

$$
\sum x_i - \sum 2 = 30 \implies \sum x_i - 2 \times 10 = 30 \implies \sum x_i = 50
$$

So, \(\frac{\sum x_i}{10} = 5\).

$$
\frac{4}{5} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{10} - (5)^2
$$

$$
\frac{4}{5} = \frac{\sum x_i^2}{10} - 25
$$

$$
\frac{\sum x_i^2}{10} = 25 + \frac{4}{5} = \frac{125+4}{5} = \frac{129}{5}
$$

$$
\implies \sum x_i^2 = 10 \times \frac{129}{5} = 2 \times 129 = 258
$$

Now, given \(\sum_{i=1}^{10} (x_i - \beta)^2 = 98\):

$$
\sum (x_i^2 - 2\beta x_i + \beta^2) = 98
$$

$$
\sum x_i^2 - 2\beta \sum x_i + \sum \beta^2 = 98
$$

$$
258 - 2\beta(50) + 10\beta^2 = 98
$$

$$
10\beta^2 - 100\beta + 258 - 98 = 0
$$

$$
10\beta^2 - 100\beta + 160 = 0
$$

$$
\beta^2 - 10\beta + 16 = 0
$$

$$
(\beta - 8)(\beta - 2) = 0
$$

\(\beta = 8\) or \(\beta = 2\). Since \(\beta > 2\), we have:

$$
\therefore \beta = 8
$$

The new observations are \(y_i = 2(x_i - 1) + 4\beta = 2x_i - 2 + 4\beta\).

The mean of the new observations is \(\mu\):

$$
\mu = E[y_i] = E[2x_i - 2 + 4\beta] = 2E[x_i] - 2 + 4\beta
$$

We know \(E[x_i] = \frac{\sum x_i}{10} = \frac{50}{10} = 5\).

$$
\mu = 2(5) - 2 + 4(8) = 10 - 2 + 32 = 40
$$

The variance of the new observations is \(\sigma^2\):

$$
\sigma^2 = Var(y_i) = Var(2x_i - 2 + 4\beta)
$$

Using the property \(Var(ax + b) = a^2 Var(x)\), where \(a=2\) and \(b = -2 + 4\beta\) (a constant):

$$
\sigma^2 = 2^2 Var(x_i) = 4 \times \frac{4}{5} = \frac{16}{5}
$$

Finally, we need to find \(\frac{\beta\mu}{\sigma^2}\):

$$
\frac{\beta\mu}{\sigma^2} = \frac{8 \times 40}{16/5} = \frac{320}{16/5} = \frac{320 \times 5}{16} = 20 \times 5 = 100
$$

questions.question: Let M and m respectively be the maximum and the minimum values of f(x) = $\begin{vmatrix}$ 1+$\$sin^2  x & $\$cos^2  x & 4$\sin$ 4x \\ $\$sin^2  x & 1+$\$cos^2  x & 4$\sin$ 4x \\ $\$sin^2  x & $\$cos^2  x & 1+4$\sin$ 4x $\end{vmatrix}$ , x $\in$ R Then $M^4 - m^4$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
Given the function:

$$
f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} 1+\sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & 4\sin 4x \\ \sin^2 x & 1+\cos^2 x & 4\sin 4x \\ \sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & 1+4\sin 4x \end{vmatrix}
$$

Apply the row operations \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\) and \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\):

$$
f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} 1+\sin^2 x & \cos^2 x & 4\sin 4x \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}
$$

Expand the determinant about \(R_1\):

$$
f(x) = (1+\sin^2 x)(1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0) - \cos^2 x(-1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot (-1)) + 4\sin 4x(-1 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot (-1))
$$

$$
f(x) = (1+\sin^2 x)(1) - \cos^2 x(-1) + 4\sin 4x(1)
$$

$$
f(x) = 1+\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x + 4\sin 4x
$$

Using the identity \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\):

$$
f(x) = 1+1 + 4\sin 4x
$$

$$
f(x) = 2 + 4\sin 4x
$$

Since \(-1 \le \sin 4x \le 1\), the maximum and minimum values of \(f(x)\) are:

Maximum value \(M = 2 + 4(1) = 6\)

Minimum value \(m = 2 + 4(-1) = -2\)

Now, we need to calculate \(M^4 - m^4\):

$$
M^4 - m^4 = (6)^4 - (-2)^4
$$

$$
M^4 - m^4 = 1296 - 16
$$

$$
M^4 - m^4 = 1280
$$

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\cos$ x($\$log_{e} ($\cos$ x))^2 $\frac{dy}{dx}$ + ($\sin$ x - 3y$\sin$ x $\$log_{e} ($\cos$ x))dx = 0 for $x \in (0, \frac{\pi}{2})$. If $y(\frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{-1}{\log_{e} 2}$, then $y(\frac{\pi}{6})$ is :
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is:

$$
\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2 \frac{dy}{dx} + (\sin x - 3y\sin x \log_{e}(\cos x)) = 0
$$

Rearranging the terms and dividing by \(dx\):

$$
\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2 \frac{dy}{dx} + \sin x - 3y\sin x \log_{e}(\cos x) = 0
$$

$$
\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2 \frac{dy}{dx} - 3y\sin x \log_{e}(\cos x) = -\sin x
$$

Divide the entire equation by \(\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2\):

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{3\sin x \log_{e}(\cos x)}{\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2} y = -\frac{\sin x}{\cos x(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2}
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{3\tan x}{\log_{e}(\cos x)} y = -\frac{\tan x}{(\log_{e}(\cos x))^2}
$$

Using the property \(\log_{e}(\cos x) = -\log_{e}(\sec x)\), we substitute this into the equation:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{3\tan x}{(-\log_{e}(\sec x))} y = -\frac{\tan x}{(-\log_{e}(\sec x))^2}
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{3\tan x}{\log_{e}(\sec x)} y = -\frac{\tan x}{(\log_{e}(\sec x))^2}
$$

This is a linear differential equation of the form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)\), where \(P(x) = \frac{3\tan x}{\log_{e}(\sec x)}\) and \(Q(x) = -\frac{\tan x}{(\log_{e}(\sec x))^2}\).

The Integrating Factor (I.F.) is given by \(e^{\int P(x)dx}\).

$$
\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \frac{3\tan x}{\log_{e}(\sec x)}dx}
$$

Let \(t = \log_{e}(\sec x)\). Then, differentiating with respect to \(x\), we get \(dt = \frac{1}{\sec x} \cdot (\sec x \tan x) dx = \tan x dx\).

$$
\int \frac{3\tan x}{\log_{e}(\sec x)}dx = \int \frac{3}{t} dt = 3\log_{e}|t| = \log_{e}|t|^3 = \log_{e}|\log_{e}(\sec x)|^3
$$

$$
\text{I.F.} = e^{\log_{e}(\log_{e}(\sec x))^3} = (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3
$$

The general solution is \(y \times \text{I.F.} = \int Q(x) \times \text{I.F.} dx + C\).

$$
y \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = \int -\frac{\tan x}{(\log_{e}(\sec x))^2} \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 dx + C
$$

$$
y \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = -\int \tan x \log_{e}(\sec x) dx + C
$$

Again, let \(t = \log_{e}(\sec x)\), so \(dt = \tan x dx\).

$$
y \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = -\int t dt + C
$$

$$
y \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = -\frac{t^2}{2} + C
$$

$$
y \times (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = -\frac{1}{2}(\log_{e}(\sec x))^2 + C
$$

Given: \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(y = \frac{-1}{\log_{e} 2}\).

At \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sec x = \sec \frac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt{2}\).

$$
\log_{e}(\sec x) = \log_{e}(\sqrt{2}) = \log_{e}(2^{1/2}) = \frac{1}{2}\log_{e} 2
$$

Substitute these values into the general solution:

$$
\frac{-1}{\log_{e} 2} \times (\frac{1}{2}\log_{e} 2)^3 = -\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\log_{e} 2)^2 + C
$$

$$
\frac{-1}{\log_{e} 2} \times \frac{1}{8}(\log_{e} 2)^3 = -\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4}(\log_{e} 2)^2 + C
$$

$$
-\frac{1}{8}(\log_{e} 2)^2 = -\frac{1}{8}(\log_{e} 2)^2 + C
$$

$$
\implies C = 0
$$

The particular solution is:

$$
y (\log_{e}(\sec x))^3 = -\frac{1}{2}(\log_{e}(\sec x))^2
$$

Since \(\log_{e}(\sec x) \neq 0\) for \(x \in (0, \frac{\pi}{2})\), we can divide by \((\log_{e}(\sec x))^2\):

$$
y = -\frac{1}{2\log_{e}(\sec x)}
$$

Now, we need to find \(y(\frac{\pi}{6})\).

At \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}\), \(\sec x = \sec \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\).

$$
y(\frac{\pi}{6}) = -\frac{1}{2\log_{e}(\sec \frac{\pi}{6})}
$$

$$
= -\frac{1}{2\log_{e}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})}
$$

$$
= -\frac{1}{2(\log_{e} 2 - \log_{e} \sqrt{3})}
$$

$$
= -\frac{1}{2(\log_{e} 2 - \frac{1}{2}\log_{e} 3)}
$$

$$
= -\frac{1}{2\log_{e} 2 - \log_{e} 3}
$$

Using the property \(n\log_{e} a = \log_{e} a^n\), we have \(2\log_{e} 2 = \log_{e} 2^2 = \log_{e} 4\).

$$
= -\frac{1}{\log_{e} 4 - \log_{e} 3}
$$

To match the options, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by -1:

$$
= \frac{1}{-(\log_{e} 4 - \log_{e} 3)}
$$

$$
= \frac{1}{\log_{e} 3 - \log_{e} 4}
$$

This matches Option (D).

questions.question: Let $|z_{1} - 8 - 2i|\leq 1$ and $|z_{2} - 2 + 6i|\leq 2$, $z_{1}, z_{2} \in C$. Then the minimum value of $|z_{1} - z_{2}|$ is :
questions.explanation:
The inequality \(|z_{1} - 8 - 2i|\leq 1\) represents a disk in the complex plane with center \(A(8, 2)\) and radius \(r_{1} = 1\).

The inequality \(|z_{2} - 2 + 6i|\leq 2\) represents a disk in the complex plane with center \(B(2, -6)\) and radius \(r_{2} = 2\).

The distance between the centers A and B is given by:

$$
AB = \sqrt{(8-2)^2 + (2-(-6))^2}
$$

$$
AB = \sqrt{(6)^2 + (8)^2}
$$

$$
AB = \sqrt{36 + 64}
$$

$$
AB = \sqrt{100}
$$

$$
AB = 10
$$

The minimum value of \(|z_{1} - z_{2}|\) is the distance between the centers minus the sum of their radii, since the disks do not overlap.

$$
|z_{1} - z_{2}|_{\min} = AB - r_{1} - r_{2}
$$

$$
|z_{1} - z_{2}|_{\min} = 10 - 1 - 2
$$

$$
|z_{1} - z_{2}|_{\min} = 7
$$

questions.question: Let ABC be a triangle formed by the lines $7x - 6y + 3 = 0$, $x + 2y - 31 = 0$ and $9x - 2y - 19 = 0$. Let the point $(h,k)$ be the image of the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ in the line $3x + 6y - 53 = 0$. Then $h^2 + k^2 + hk$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
$$
\therefore \text{centroid of } \triangle ABC = \left(\frac{9+3+5}{3}, \frac{11+4+13}{3}\right)
$$

$$
= \left(\frac{17}{3}, \frac{28}{3}\right)
$$

Let the point \((h,k)\) be the image of the centroid \(\left(\frac{17}{3}, \frac{28}{3}\right)\) in the line \(3x + 6y - 53 = 0\).

The line joining the centroid and its image is perpendicular to the mirror line \(3x + 6y - 53 = 0\). The slope of the mirror line is \(m_L = -\frac{3}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, the slope of the line joining the centroid and its image is \(m_{GI} = -\frac{1}{m_L} = 2\). This gives the first equation:

$$
\frac{k - \frac{28}{3}}{h - \frac{17}{3}} \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -1 \quad \text{(1)}
$$

The midpoint of the segment joining the centroid and its image lies on the mirror line. The midpoint is \(\left(\frac{h + \frac{17}{3}}{2}, \frac{k + \frac{28}{3}}{2}\right)\). Substituting this into the line equation \(3x + 6y - 53 = 0\) gives the second equation:

$$
3\left(\frac{h + \frac{17}{3}}{2}\right) + 6\left(\frac{k + \frac{28}{3}}{2}\right) = 53 \quad \text{(2)}
$$

Solving (1) & (2) we get \(h = 3, k = 4\).

$$
\therefore h^2 + k^2 + hk = 3^2 + 4^2 + 3 \times 4 = 9 + 16 + 12 = 37
$$

questions.question: Two parabolas have the same focus $(4,3)$ and their directrices are the x-axis and the y-axis, respectively. If these parabolas intersect at the points A and B, then $(AB)^2$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
A parabola is defined as the locus of a point that moves such that its distance from a fixed point (focus) is equal to its distance from a fixed line (directrix).

Given focus \(S(4,3)\).

For Parabola I, the directrix is the x-axis (equation \(y=0\)).

$$
\sqrt{(x-4)^2 + (y-3)^2} = |y|
$$

$$
(x-4)^2 + (y-3)^2 = y^2 \quad \ldots(1)
$$

For Parabola II, the directrix is the y-axis (equation \(x=0\)).

$$
\sqrt{(x-4)^2 + (y-3)^2} = |x|
$$

$$
(x-4)^2 + (y-3)^2 = x^2 \quad \ldots(2)
$$

Let the intersection points be \(A(x_1, y_1)\) and \(B(x_2, y_2)\). These points satisfy both equations (1) and (2).

Equating the right-hand sides of (1) and (2):

$$
y^2 = x^2
$$

$$
y = \pm x
$$

From the diagram, the intersection points are in the first quadrant, so we consider \(y=x\).

$$
y = x \quad \ldots(3)
$$

Substitute \(y=x\) into equation (1):

$$
(x-4)^2 + (x-3)^2 = x^2
$$

$$
x^2 - 8x + 16 + x^2 - 6x + 9 = x^2
$$

$$
x^2 - 14x + 25 = 0
$$

Let the roots of this quadratic equation be \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). These are the x-coordinates of points A and B. By Vieta's formulas:

$$
x_1 + x_2 = 14
$$

$$
x_1 x_2 = 25
$$

Since \(y=x\), the y-coordinates are \(y_1 = x_1\) and \(y_2 = x_2\).

The square of the distance between points A and B is given by the distance formula:

$$
(AB)^2 = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2
$$

Substitute \(y_1 = x_1\) and \(y_2 = x_2\):

$$
(AB)^2 = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + (x_1 - x_2)^2
$$

$$
(AB)^2 = 2(x_1 - x_2)^2
$$

Using the identity \((x_1 - x_2)^2 = (x_1 + x_2)^2 - 4x_1 x_2\):

$$
(AB)^2 = 2[(x_1 + x_2)^2 - 4x_1 x_2]
$$

Substitute the values \(x_1 + x_2 = 14\) and \(x_1 x_2 = 25\):

$$
(AB)^2 = 2[(14)^2 - 4(25)]
$$

$$
(AB)^2 = 2[196 - 100]
$$

$$
(AB)^2 = 2[96]
$$

$$
(AB)^2 = 192
$$

questions.question: Let the ellipse, $E_1 : \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, a $\gt$ b and $E_2 : \frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = 1$, A $\lt$ B have same eccentricity $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ . Let the product of their lengths of latus rectums be $\frac{32}{\sqrt{3}}$ , and the distance between the foci of $E_1$ be 4. If $E_1$ and $E_2$ meet at A,B,C and D, then the area of the quadrilateral ABCD equals:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For ellipse \(E_1 : \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) with a \gt b:

Distance between foci is \(2ae = 4\).

Given eccentricity \(e = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

$$
2a\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = 4
$$

$$
\Rightarrow a = 2\sqrt{3}
$$

Using the relation \(e^2 = 1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}\):

$$
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{b^2}{(2\sqrt{3})^2}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{3} = 1 - \frac{b^2}{12}
$$

$$
\frac{b^2}{12} = 1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow b^2 = 8
$$

The length of the latus rectum for \(E_1\) is \(L_1 = \frac{2b^2}{a} = \frac{2(8)}{2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}\).

For ellipse \(E_2 : \frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = 1\) with A \lt B:

The major axis is along the y-axis. The eccentricity is given by \(e^2 = 1 - \frac{A^2}{B^2}\).

Given eccentricity \(e = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

$$
\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{A^2}{B^2}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{3} = 1 - \frac{A^2}{B^2}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \frac{A^2}{B^2} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

The length of the latus rectum for \(E_2\) is \(L_2 = \frac{2A^2}{B}\).

The product of their lengths of latus rectums is given as \(\frac{32}{\sqrt{3}}\).

$$
L_1 \cdot L_2 = \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\left(\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{2A^2}{B}\right) = \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
\frac{16A^2}{B\sqrt{3}} = \frac{32}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
16A^2 = 32B
$$

$$
\Rightarrow A^2 = 2B
$$

Substitute \(A^2 = 2B\) into the equation \(\frac{A^2}{B^2} = \frac{2}{3}\):

$$
\frac{2B}{B^2} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

$$
\frac{2}{B} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow B = 3
$$

Now find \(A^2\):

$$
A^2 = 2B = 2(3) = 6
$$

The equations of the ellipses are:

$$
E_1: \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{x^2}{12} + \frac{y^2}{8} = 1 \quad \text{.....(1)}
$$

$$
E_2: \frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{x^2}{6} + \frac{y^2}{9} = 1 \quad \text{.....(2)}
$$

To find the intersection points, we solve equations (1) and (2) simultaneously.

$$
\text{From (1): } 2x^2 + 3y^2 = 24 \quad (\text{multiplying by 24})
$$

$$
\text{From (2): } 3x^2 + 2y^2 = 18 \quad (\text{multiplying by 18})
$$

Multiply the first new equation by 2 and the second by 3:

$$
4x^2 + 6y^2 = 48
$$

$$
9x^2 + 6y^2 = 54
$$

Subtract the first from the second:

$$
(9x^2 + 6y^2) - (4x^2 + 6y^2) = 54 - 48
$$

$$
5x^2 = 6 \Rightarrow x^2 = \frac{6}{5} \Rightarrow x = \pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}} = \pm \frac{\sqrt{30}}{5}
$$

Substitute \(x^2 = \frac{6}{5}\) into \(3x^2 + 2y^2 = 18\):

$$
3\left(\frac{6}{5}\right) + 2y^2 = 18
$$

$$
\frac{18}{5} + 2y^2 = 18
$$

$$
2y^2 = 18 - \frac{18}{5} = \frac{90 - 18}{5} = \frac{72}{5}
$$

$$
y^2 = \frac{36}{5} \Rightarrow y = \pm \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}} = \pm \frac{6\sqrt{5}}{5}
$$

The four intersection points (A, B, C, D) are:

$$
\left(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\right), \left(-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\right), \left(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}, -\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\right), \left(-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}, -\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\right)
$$

These four points form a rectangle with vertices at \((\pm x_0, \pm y_0)\), where \(x_0 = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}\) and \(y_0 = \frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\).

The length of the rectangle is \(2x_0 = 2\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}\).

The width of the rectangle is \(2y_0 = 2\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\).

Area of the quadrilateral ABCD (rectangle) = Length \(\times\) Width

$$
\text{Area} = \left(2\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{5}}\right) \times \left(2\frac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\right)
$$

$$
\text{Area} = \frac{4 \times 6\sqrt{6}}{5} = \frac{24\sqrt{6}}{5}
$$

questions.question: Let the area of the region $\{(x,y): 2y \leq x^2 + 3, y + |x| \leq 3, y \geq |x-1|\}$ be A. Then 6A is equal to:
questions.explanation:
### Solution for Area Calculation

The region A is defined by the inequalities \(2y \leq x^2 + 3\), \(y + |x| \leq 3\), and \(y \geq |x-1|\). These inequalities can be rewritten as:

• \(y \leq \frac{x^2+3}{2}\)
• \(y \leq 3-|x|\)
• \(y \geq |x-1|\)

The region of integration is shown in the diagram below, with key points and boundary equations labeled. The shaded region represents A.

The area A can be calculated by subtracting the area of a specific region from a larger area. Based on the geometry and symmetry, the area A is given by:

$$
A = 4 - 2 \int_{0}^{1} \left( (3-x) - \left(\frac{x^2+3}{2}\right) \right) dx
$$

First, simplify the integrand:

$$
\left( (3-x) - \left(\frac{x^2+3}{2}\right) \right) = 3-x - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{3}{2} = -\frac{x^2}{2} - x + \frac{3}{2}
$$

Now, perform the integration:

$$
2 \int_{0}^{1} \left( -\frac{x^2}{2} - x + \frac{3}{2} \right) dx = 2 \left[ -\frac{x^3}{6} - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{3x}{2} \right]_{0}^{1}
$$

$$
= 2 \left( \left( -\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{2} \right) - (0) \right)
$$

$$
= 2 \left( -\frac{1}{6} + 1 \right) = 2 \left( \frac{5}{6} \right) = \frac{5}{3}
$$

Substitute this value back into the expression for A:

$$
A = 4 - \frac{5}{3} = \frac{12-5}{3} = \frac{7}{3}
$$

The question asks for the value of 6A.

$$
6A = 6 \times \frac{7}{3} = 2 \times 7 = 14
$$

questions.question:
Let $A = [a_{ij}] =  \begin{bmatrix} \$log_5  128 & $\$log_4  5 \\ $\$log_5  8 & $\$log_4  25 $\end{bmatrix}$
If $A_{ij}$ is the cofactor of $a_{ij}$, $C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{ik} A_{jk}$, $1 \le i, j \le 2$, and $C = [C_{ij}]$, then $8|C|$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \log_5 128 & \log_4 5 \\ \log_5 8 & \log_4 25 \end{bmatrix}\).

First, simplify the logarithmic terms using \(\log_b (x^n) = n \log_b x\) and \(\log_b a = \frac{\log_c a}{\log_c b}\):

$$
\log_5 128 = \log_5 (2^7) = 7 \log_5 2
$$

$$
\log_5 8 = \log_5 (2^3) = 3 \log_5 2
$$

$$
\log_4 25 = \log_4 (5^2) = 2 \log_4 5
$$

Now, substitute these into matrix A:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \log_5 2 & \log_4 5 \\ 3 \log_5 2 & 2 \log_4 5 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Calculate the determinant \(|A|\):

$$
|A| = (7 \log_5 2)(2 \log_4 5) - (\log_4 5)(3 \log_5 2)
$$

$$
|A| = 14 (\log_5 2)(\log_4 5) - 3 (\log_5 2)(\log_4 5)
$$

$$
|A| = 11 (\log_5 2)(\log_4 5)
$$

Using the change of base property \((\log_b a)(\log_a c) = \log_b c\) or \((\log_b a)(\log_c b) = \log_c a\):

$$
(\log_5 2)(\log_4 5) = (\log_5 2) \left(\frac{\log_5 5}{\log_5 4}\right) = (\log_5 2) \left(\frac{1}{\log_5 (2^2)}\right)
$$

$$
= (\log_5 2) \left(\frac{1}{2 \log_5 2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, \(|A| = 11 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{11}{2}\).

The elements of matrix \(C\) are defined as \(C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{ik} A_{jk}\), where \(A_{jk}\) is the cofactor of \(a_{jk}\).

This is a standard property of determinants: the sum of the products of the elements of any row (or column) with the cofactors of the corresponding elements of the same row (or column) is equal to the determinant of the matrix. If the cofactors are taken from a different row (or column), the sum is zero.

$$
C_{11} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{1k} A_{1k} = a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} = |A| = \frac{11}{2}
$$

$$
C_{12} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{1k} A_{2k} = a_{11}A_{21} + a_{12}A_{22} = 0 \quad (\text{elements of row 1 with cofactors of row 2})
$$

$$
C_{21} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{2k} A_{1k} = a_{21}A_{11} + a_{22}A_{12} = 0 \quad (\text{elements of row 2 with cofactors of row 1})
$$

$$
C_{22} = \sum_{k=1}^{2} a_{2k} A_{2k} = a_{21}A_{21} + a_{22}A_{22} = |A| = \frac{11}{2}
$$

So, the matrix \(C\) is:

$$
C = \begin{bmatrix} 11/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 11/2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The determinant of \(C\) is:

$$
|C| = \left(\frac{11}{2}\right) \left(\frac{11}{2}\right) - (0)(0) = \frac{121}{4}
$$

Finally, calculate \(8|C|\):

$$
8|C| = 8 \cdot \frac{121}{4} = 2 \cdot 121 = 242
$$

questions.question: Let $[t]$ be the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Then the least value of $p \in N$ for which $\lim$_{x \to $0^{+}$} $\left(x\left(\left[\frac{1}{x}\right] + \left[\frac{2}{x}\right]$+....+$\left[\frac{p}{x}\right] \right$)-$x^{2} \left(\left[\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right] + \left[\frac{2^{2}}{x^{2}}\right]$+....+$\left[\frac{9^{2}}{x^{2}}\right] \right$)$\right$)$\ge$ 1 is equal to $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$ .
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The given limit expression is:

$$
\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \left(x\left(\left[\frac{1}{x}\right]+\left[\frac{2}{x}\right]+....+\left[\frac{p}{x}\right]\right)-x^{2}\left(\left[\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right]+\left[\frac{2^{2}}{x^{2}}\right]+....+\left[\frac{9^{2}}{x^{2}}\right]\right)\right)\ge 1
$$

We use the property that for \(k > 0\), \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} x\left[\frac{k}{x}\right] = k\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} x^{2}\left[\frac{k}{x^{2}}\right] = k\).

Applying this property to the expression:

$$
(1 + 2 + .....+ p) - (1^{2} + 2^{2} + ....+9^{2}) \ge 1
$$

Using the sum formulas for arithmetic progression and sum of squares:

$$
\frac{p(p+1)}{2} - \frac{9(9+1)(2 \cdot 9+1)}{6} \ge 1
$$

$$
\frac{p(p+1)}{2} - \frac{9 \cdot 10 \cdot 19}{6} \ge 1
$$

$$
\frac{p(p+1)}{2} - (3 \cdot 5 \cdot 19) \ge 1
$$

$$
\frac{p(p+1)}{2} - 285 \ge 1
$$

$$
\frac{p(p+1)}{2} \ge 286
$$

$$
p(p+1) \ge 572
$$

We need to find the least natural value of \(p\) that satisfies this inequality.

If \(p=23\), then \(p(p+1) = 23 \times 24 = 552\), which is not \(\ge 572\).

If \(p=24\), then \(p(p+1) = 24 \times 25 = 600\), which is \(\ge 572\).

Therefore, the least natural value of \(p\) is 24.

questions.question: Let $S = \{x : \cos^{-1} x = \pi + \sin^{-1} x + \sin^{-1} (2x + 1)\}$. Then $\sum_{x\in S} (2x-1)^2$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation:
Given the equation:

$$
\cos^{-1}x = \pi + \sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}(2x+1)
$$

Rearranging the terms:

$$
\cos^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}(2x+1) = \pi
$$

We know that \(\cos^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}\). So, \(\cos^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}x\).

$$
\frac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}(2x+1) = \pi
$$

$$
\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\sin^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}(2x+1) = \pi
$$

$$
-2\sin^{-1}x - \sin^{-1}(2x+1) = \frac{\pi}{2}
$$

$$
2\sin^{-1}x + \sin^{-1}(2x+1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}
$$

Let \(\cos^{-1}x = \alpha\) and \(\sin^{-1}(2x+1) = \beta\).

From the original equation, we have:

$$
\alpha = \pi + (\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha) + \beta
$$

$$
\alpha = \frac{3\pi}{2} - \alpha + \beta
$$

$$
2\alpha - \beta = \frac{3\pi}{2}
$$

This implies:

$$
2\alpha = \frac{3\pi}{2} + \beta
$$

Taking cosine on both sides (or using \(\cos(2\alpha) = \sin(\beta)\) from the solution's approach):

The domain of \(\cos^{-1}x\) is \([-1, 1]\), so \(x \in [-1, 1]\).

The domain of \(\sin^{-1}(2x+1)\) is \([-1, 1]\), so \(-1 \le 2x+1 \le 1 \Rightarrow -2 \le 2x \le 0 \Rightarrow -1 \le x \le 0\).

Combining these, \(x \in [-1, 0]\).

Also, \(\alpha \in [0, \pi]\) and \(\beta \in [-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]\).

From \(2\alpha - \beta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\):

Since \(x \in [-1, 0]\), \(\alpha = \cos^{-1}x \in [\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi]\).

So \(2\alpha \in [\pi, 2\pi]\).

Since \(x \in [-1, 0]\), \(2x+1 \in [-1, 1]\), so \(\beta = \sin^{-1}(2x+1) \in [-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]\).

From \(2\alpha - \beta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\), the maximum value of \(2\alpha - \beta\) is \(2\pi - (-\frac{\pi}{2}) = \frac{5\pi}{2}\) and the minimum value is \(\pi - \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

The equation \(2\alpha - \beta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\) is consistent with the ranges.

From the solution steps provided:

$$
\cos(2\alpha) = \sin\beta
$$

$$
2\cos^2\alpha - 1 = \sin\beta
$$

Substitute \(\cos\alpha = x\) and \(\sin\beta = 2x+1\):

$$
2x^2 - 1 = 2x + 1
$$

$$
2x^2 - 2x - 2 = 0
$$

$$
x^2 - x - 1 = 0
$$

Solving the quadratic equation for \(x\):

$$
x = \frac{-(-1) \pm \sqrt{(-1)^2 - 4(1)(-1)}}{2(1)} = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1+4}}{2} = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}
$$

We have two possible values for \(x\):

$$
\begin{cases} x = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} & \text{rejected} \\ x = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \end{cases}
$$

The value \(x = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx \frac{1+2.236}{2} = 1.618\) is rejected because it is not in the domain \(x \in [-1, 0]\).

The value \(x = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx \frac{1-2.236}{2} = -0.618\) is in the domain \(x \in [-1, 0]\).

So, the set S contains only one element: \(x = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\).

We need to find \(\sum_{x\in S} (2x-1)^2\). Since S has only one element, this is just \((2x-1)^2\) for \(x = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\).

From \(x^2 - x - 1 = 0\), we can multiply by 4:

$$
4x^2 - 4x - 4 = 0
$$

$$
4x^2 - 4x = 4
$$

Now consider the expression \((2x-1)^2\):

$$
(2x-1)^2 = (2x)^2 - 2(2x)(1) + 1^2 = 4x^2 - 4x + 1
$$

Substitute \(4x^2 - 4x = 4\) into the expression:

$$
(2x-1)^2 = 4 + 1 = 5
$$

questions.question: Let $f : (0,\infty) \to R$ be a twice differentiable function. If for some $a \neq 0$, $\int_{0}^{1} f(\lambda x)d\lambda = af(x)$, $f(1) = 1$ and $f(16) = \frac{1}{8}$, then $16-f' \left$($\frac{1}{16} \right$)$$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation:
Given integral equation:

$$
\int_{0}^{1} f(\lambda x)d\lambda = af(x)
$$

Let \(\lambda x = t\). Then \(x d\lambda = dt \implies d\lambda = \frac{1}{x}dt\).

When \(\lambda = 0, t = 0\).

When \(\lambda = 1, t = x\).

Substituting these into the integral:

$$
\int_{0}^{x} f(t) \frac{1}{x} dt = af(x)
$$

$$
\frac{1}{x} \int_{0}^{x} f(t)dt = af(x)
$$

$$
\int_{0}^{x} f(t)dt = axf(x)
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\) (using Leibniz integral rule on the left side and product rule on the right side):

$$
f(x) = a(1 \cdot f(x) + x f'(x))
$$

$$
f(x) = af(x) + axf'(x)
$$

$$
(1-a)f(x) = axf'(x)
$$

Rearranging to form a separable differential equation:

$$
\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{1-a}{a} \frac{1}{x}
$$

Integrating both sides:

$$
\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} dx = \int \frac{1-a}{a} \frac{1}{x} dx
$$

$$
\ln|f(x)| = \frac{1-a}{a} \ln|x| + C
$$

Since \(x \in (0, \infty)\), \(|x| = x\). Given \(f(1)=1\), we can assume \(f(x) > 0\) for the domain of interest.

$$
\ln f(x) = \frac{1-a}{a} \ln x + C
$$

Using the condition \(f(1) = 1\):

$$
\ln 1 = \frac{1-a}{a} \ln 1 + C \implies 0 = 0 + C \implies C = 0
$$

So, the function is:

$$
\ln f(x) = \frac{1-a}{a} \ln x
$$

$$
f(x) = x^{\frac{1-a}{a}}
$$

Using the condition \(f(16) = \frac{1}{8}\):

$$
\frac{1}{8} = (16)^{\frac{1-a}{a}}
$$

$$
2^{-3} = (2^4)^{\frac{1-a}{a}}
$$

$$
2^{-3} = 2^{\frac{4(1-a)}{a}}
$$

Equating the exponents:

$$
-3 = \frac{4(1-a)}{a}
$$

$$
-3a = 4 - 4a
$$

$$
a = 4
$$

Substitute \(a=4\) back into the expression for \(f(x)\):

$$
f(x) = x^{\frac{1-4}{4}} = x^{-\frac{3}{4}}
$$

Now, find the derivative \(f'(x)\):

$$
f'(x) = -\frac{3}{4} x^{-\frac{3}{4}-1} = -\frac{3}{4} x^{-\frac{7}{4}}
$$

Evaluate \(f'\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)\):

$$
f'\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) = -\frac{3}{4} \left(\frac{1}{16}\right)^{-\frac{7}{4}}
$$

$$
= -\frac{3}{4} (16)^{\frac{7}{4}}
$$

$$
= -\frac{3}{4} (2^4)^{\frac{7}{4}}
$$

$$
= -\frac{3}{4} (2^7)
$$

$$
= -\frac{3}{4} (128)
$$

$$
= -3 \times 32 = -96
$$

Finally, calculate \(16 - f'\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)\):

$$
16 - f'\left(\frac{1}{16}\right) = 16 - (-96)
$$

$$
= 16 + 96 = 112
$$

questions.question: Let $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be a vector such that $\vec{a} \times \vec{c} = \vec{c} \times \vec{b}$ and $(\vec{a} + \vec{c}) \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 168$. Then the maximum value of $|\vec{c}|^2$ is:
questions.explanation:
Given vectors are \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}\).

We are given the condition \(\vec{a} \times \vec{c} = \vec{c} \times \vec{b}\).

$$
\vec{a} \times \vec{c} - \vec{c} \times \vec{b} = 0
$$

Since \(\vec{c} \times \vec{b} = -(\vec{b} \times \vec{c})\), we can write:

$$
\vec{a} \times \vec{c} + \vec{b} \times \vec{c} = 0
$$

$$
(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \times \vec{c} = 0
$$

This implies that \(\vec{c}\) is parallel to \((\vec{a} + \vec{b})\). So, we can write \(\vec{c} = \lambda (\vec{a} + \vec{b})\) for some scalar \(\lambda\).

First, calculate \(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\):

$$
\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) + (3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}) = (2+3)\hat{i} + (-1-5)\hat{j} + (3+1)\hat{k} = 5\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}
$$

So, \(\vec{c} = \lambda (5\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})\) .....(1)

Now, calculate \(|\vec{c}|^2\):

$$
|\vec{c}|^2 = \lambda^2 (5^2 + (-6)^2 + 4^2) = \lambda^2 (25 + 36 + 16) = 77\lambda^2
$$

Next, use the second given condition: \((\vec{a} + \vec{c}) \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 168\).

Expand the dot product:

$$
\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} + \vec{c} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{c}|^2 = 168
$$

Calculate \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}\):

$$
\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = (2)(3) + (-1)(-5) + (3)(1) = 6 + 5 + 3 = 14
$$

Substitute \(\vec{c} = \lambda (\vec{a} + \vec{b})\) into \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} + \vec{c} \cdot \vec{b}\):

$$
\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} + \vec{c} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b})
$$

Using equation (1):

$$
\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = \lambda (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = \lambda |\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2
$$

We know \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = 77\), so \(\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = 77\lambda\).

Substitute these values back into the expanded dot product equation:

$$
14 + 77\lambda + 77\lambda^2 = 168
$$

Rearrange the equation:

$$
77\lambda^2 + 77\lambda - 154 = 0
$$

Divide by 77:

$$
\lambda^2 + \lambda - 2 = 0
$$

Factor the quadratic equation:

$$
(\lambda + 2)(\lambda - 1) = 0
$$

This gives two possible values for \(\lambda\): \(\lambda = -2\) or \(\lambda = 1\).

We need to find the maximum value of \(|\vec{c}|^2\), which is \(77\lambda^2\).

If \(\lambda = -2\):

$$
|\vec{c}|^2 = 77(-2)^2 = 77 \times 4 = 308
$$

If \(\lambda = 1\):

$$
|\vec{c}|^2 = 77(1)^2 = 77 \times 1 = 77
$$

The maximum value of \(|\vec{c}|^2\) is 308.
